title: Old-Time Firewood Wisdom
subtitle: Old Farm Woodpile Know-How
items: Cut and split a year ahead
Stack bark side up, off ground
Face the pile to sun and wind
Keep main pile off the house
intro: Old farm families cut next winter's wood this winter. Dry, seasoned wood lights easier, gives more heat and leaves less creosote in the chimney. Here is the old woodpile know-how in our own words.
desc: Old-time firewood wisdom for homesteaders: cut and split wood a year ahead, stack it off the ground with the top covered and sides open to sun and wind, and burn only dry seasoned wood for more heat and less chimney creosote. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Pressure Can Sweet Potatoes
subtitle: USDA-Tested Method
intro: Home-canned sweet potatoes are ready for a quick side dish or pie filling all winter. They are low-acid, so they must be pressure canned; these steps follow the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning.
desc: How to pressure can sweet potatoes the USDA way: boil until partly soft, peel and cut into pieces (never mash or puree), hot pack with boiling water or light syrup and 1-inch headspace, then process pints 65 minutes and quarts 90 minutes at 10 lb weighted or 11 lb dial gauge pressure, adjusting for altitude. Full list on the blog.

title: Regrow Green Onions Indoors
subtitle: Free Greens on the Windowsill
items: Save 1-2 in. of the white root
Set roots in a glass of water
Set it in your sunniest window
Move to a pot of soil to last
intro: Green onions are the easiest winter windowsill crop: the root ends from a store bunch will send up new greens within days. It is a fun first step into growing food indoors.
desc: How to regrow green onions (scallions) indoors in winter: stand the white root ends in a glass of water in a sunny window, change the water every day or two, snip the greens as they grow and move them to soil for a longer harvest. Full list on the blog.

title: Raised Bed Planning Checklist
subtitle: Get Ready for Spring Now
items: Pick a spot with 6-8 hrs sun
Keep beds 4 ft wide or less
Tall crops on the north side
Add compost on top every year
desc: Raised bed planning checklist for beginner vegetable gardeners: choose a spot with 6-8 hours of sun, keep beds no wider than 4 feet so you can reach the middle, give roots 10-12 inches of soil and fill with a topsoil and compost mix. Plan this winter, build in spring. (Contains affiliate links.)

title: How to Freeze Cauliflower
subtitle: Blanch, Chill, Pack
intro: Cauliflower freezes well if you blanch it first; blanching stops the enzymes that turn frozen vegetables gray and tough. Frozen florets go straight into soups, casseroles and roasting pans.
desc: How to freeze cauliflower so it stays white and firm: break heads into 1-inch florets, blanch 3 minutes in water with 4 teaspoons of salt per gallon, chill in ice water, drain and pack in freezer bags or containers. Full list on the blog.

title: Best Cold-Hardy Chicken Breeds
subtitle: Hens That Handle Winter
intro: If your winters are cold, start with breeds that are heavy, well-feathered and have small combs that resist frostbite. These classic dual-purpose hens keep going when the water bucket freezes.
desc: Best cold-hardy chicken breeds for backyard flocks: Wyandottes, Plymouth Rocks, Buff Orpingtons, Australorps, Brahmas and Chanteclers are heavy, well-feathered hens, and small rose or pea combs resist frostbite. Full list on the blog.
